articles.title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
paras: A volcanic eruption in the shallows near Iwo Jima has extended the Japanese island’s famed black sand beaches, at least temporarily.
Signs of unrest began in late October 2026.
On October 27, seismic sensors recorded a sharp uptick in activity, and Japan’s Meteorological Agency reported that the first photographs of the eruption were captured.
Soon after, sensors on several satellites began to capture an array of observations.
The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured the left image on October 26, when the coast was still quiet.
On November 11, Landsat 9 got its first clear view of the land the submarine volcano has built (right).
A shortwave-infrared signature, a sign of the eruption’s heat, is shown in orange.
A faint gray volcanic plume drifts southeast of the vent, and a streak of floating pumice stretches across the water in the same direction.
A false-color backscatter radar image from the NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite offered an even earlier look at the eruption.
On October 28, despite heavy cloud cover, the radar detected a large disturbance in the water in the same area that erupted in December 2023.

When the clouds cleared in early November, the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) and VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) sensors on NASA and NOAA satellites also captured signs of the ongoing eruption’s volcanic plumes and infrared signature .
Japan’s Coast Guard released a report on November 16 confirming the formation of new land connected to the pre-existing beach.
The eruption appears to have added roughly 50 hectares (125 acres) of new beach, about the area of 90 American football fields.
That would enlarge the island by about 1.7 percent.
The new land adjoins the southeast beach where American troops landed on February 19, 1945, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the history of the U.S.
Marines.
The location of the eruption is no surprise to scientists.
In addition to the 2023 eruption off the southeast coast, Iwo Jima had an eruption off its west coast in August 2025, said Daniel Slayback, a scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
How long the new land will persist remains an open question.
New land created by the 2023 eruption succumbed to wave action after just a few weeks, Slayback said.
New land on volcanic islands has persisted more than a decade only a handful of times in recent times, including at Capelinhos, Surtsey, McDonald Island, and Home Reef, he added.
“I imagine we’ll see this new land wash away within a few months,” he said.
“But we’ll have to wait and see.”

Among the scientists watching closely is James Garvin, the chief scientist at Goddard and a geologist with a long-standing interest in how underwater volcanic eruptions create new islands and other landforms.
Typically, tephra -dominated eruptions like this form new land that is quickly “attacked” by ocean waves and other hydrologic forces, Garvin explained.
An exception is when the eruption also injects certain types of lava that “cement” the ash into stronger material.
“If we do see injection of basaltic-andesitic lava within the new materials, then it’s possible the new land could follow a pattern different from what we monitored in 2023,” he said.

NISAR will be especially valuable for tracking the site, Garvin said, because it makes frequent, high-resolution interferometric observations through clouds and can show whether the new land erodes, subsides, or grows.
The satellite has already recorded major changes at the eruption site between October 28 and November 11 .
NASA scientists will also analyze sub-meter-resolution imagery from commercial satellites through NASA’s Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program .
These images can reveal subtle deformation features like rilles, fractures, and cracks that offer clues about the stability of the new land.
Both Slayback and Garvin have studied new volcanic land before.

They were part of a team that monitored new land in the Kingdom of Tonga after an eruption in the Southwest Pacific but before most of it was obliterated during the highly explosive Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai caldera collapse and eruption in January 2022.

Geological Survey .

articles.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
paras: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.
Experts from across the agency, the U.S.
Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October.
Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.
“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director.
“This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”
Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall , a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars.
Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.

As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable.

SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future Moon Base , and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.

The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s Ignition event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.
One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations.
The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element.
The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.
NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft.
This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.
Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its nuclear power module , and how long its reactor will operate.
These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.
In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s Power and Propulsion Element by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars.
SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth.
Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.
NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module.
The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently.

The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.

Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight.

The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.
Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.
After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power.
The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down.
During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth.
Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.
After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space.

“By refining the design and advancing this architecture, we’re not just building a spacecraft, we’re establishing the foundation for a new era of reliable, efficient transport beyond Earth orbit,” Sinacore said.
“What we learn from SR-1 Freedom will shape the future of exploration for decades to come.”
With key design decisions advancing and teams across NASA, DOE, and industry working together, SR-1 Freedom is moving toward its 2028 launch goal.
The mission will demonstrate new capabilities for nuclear-powered transportation and help establish the foundation for future exploration beyond Earth.

articles.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
paras: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington.
“Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started.

With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon.
Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more.
NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s website .

Earlier this year during its Ignition event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of Artemis missions to the lunar surface, and building the first Moon Base , among other agency priorities.

Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.

articles.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
paras: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars.
When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova .
These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements.
Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky.
But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project!
Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.
When gravitational wave detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light.
The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.
The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents.
Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories.
They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time.
Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers.
Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar Impact Flash! project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon.
The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope .

“Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics.
“The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data.
We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively.
And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.”
The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA).
Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers.
They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding.
This science could not be done without their contributions.”
To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/ or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com .
Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!
Use your backyard telescope to spot the most cataclysmic collisions in our Universe!

articles.title: NASA Seeks Partners to Design First Nuclear Reactor for the Moon
paras: NASA is seeking industry partners to develop and test the first nuclear reactor designed to provide electricity on the Moon, a major step toward establishing a sustained human presence on the lunar surface.
Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1) will be a small fission power system that will generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth.
For NASA’s plans for a Moon Base , that energy could support future habitats, communications systems, rovers, scientific instruments, and other essential infrastructure.
NASA aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and operate it on the Moon for at least five years after deployment.
Unlike solar power, which depends on sunlight, a nuclear reactor can generate electricity continuously, including during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights.
This capability will enable future lunar operations, particularly in locations where sunlight is limited or unavailable.

“This request for proposals represents an important step forward as NASA partners with industry to establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface,” said Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager.
“A reliable source of safe and abundant energy will be vital to future exploration of the lunar and Martian surface.
Space nuclear systems will provide continuous power to NASA assets in any environment without dependency on sunlight.”

NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback received after the agency released a draft proposal in August and hosted an industry day in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland.
The solicitation requires that the reactor must meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations.

While the primary purpose of the Request for Proposals is to advance the technology, testing, and flight design of LR-1, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems.
Proposals are due by Dec. 21.
Nuclear power will be increasingly important to NASA’s space exploration ambitions.
Lunar nights last about 14 Earth days, while dust storms on Mars can block sunlight for months.
Farther from the Sun, solar power becomes progressively less effective.
Nuclear systems offer a reliable source of electricity in these challenging environments.
LR-1 is managed by the agency’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the Department of Energy.
The division is also responsible for the development of NASA’s Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom.

Scheduled to launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, which uses electricity generated by a nuclear reactor to power spacecraft propulsion systems.
This technology could enable future spacecraft to travel farther and undertake deep space missions that aren’t possible using conventional propulsion.
Together, LR-1 and SR-1 Freedom are advancing nuclear power and propulsion technologies to enable a new era of space exploration.
By investing in these technologies, NASA and DOE are helping secure America’s leadership in space for decades to come.

articles.title: NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
paras: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million.
The period of performance runs from Nov. 23 through April 1, 2042.
The work will take place at the awardee’s facility.

Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders.
NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is managing the acquisition, and NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the data to users worldwide.
Microwave sounders provide critical measurements of temperature and moisture in the atmosphere, which significantly influence weather patterns.
The SMBA instruments could improve the medium-range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.
The NEON mission is a collaboration between NASA and NOAA.
The mission is led by NOAA, which provides funding, technical requirements, and postlaunch operations.
NASA will manage the development of the NEON satellites and launch them for NOAA.
NASA and NOAA will work with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

articles.title: 65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson
paras: For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years.

Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.
Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth.
Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.
When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away.

Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued.
The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk.
Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program.

Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968.
Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface.
Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.”
Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world.
After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026.
Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science ( ARES ) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Skylab and Apollo-Soyuz: Learning to Live and Work in Space Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one.

In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew.

The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.
In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project.
Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

The Space Shuttle: Setting the Stage for Long-Duration Spaceflight Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972.
During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program.
Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions.
The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a new era of reusable spacecraft.
The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations.

Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory.
The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety.
The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011.

The Space Station: 26 Years of Continuous Human Presence An Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993.
Overall management of the program resides at Johnson.
The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module.

The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit.

To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth.
Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground.
Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners.
Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures.
At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools.

Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions.

What began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration.
The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars.
Artemis and Moon Base: Building a Sustained Lunar Presence The Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft.
The four-person crew launched April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon.
At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before.
The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions.

Building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin.
Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV.
NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole.
The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations.
Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon.
Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science.
At Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions.

From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs.

articles.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
paras: More Content About Search Even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific.
On November 15, 2026 , the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands.
Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades.

Named Xavier , the system intensified rapidly , thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones .
Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati , a short-lived storm that emerged in October.

As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June .

When the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour.

Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale .
The storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach .

Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years.
Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace .
According to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands.
It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa.
Xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months.

A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Service projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line.
Storm activity in the Southwest Pacific basin typically peaks in February .

articles.title: New NASA Seed Funding Primes Small Businesses for Innovation
paras: Awards to small businesses around the country are addressing some of NASA’s most crucial technology needs for exploration of the Moon and Mars while fueling the U.S. space economy.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research/Small Business Technology Transfer (SBIR/STTR) program recently selected 302 innovative projects, for a total investment of up to $171 million in seed funding.
This early-stage research and development work will tackle an array of topics, including those related to Artemis and the establishment of a U.S.
Moon Base .

Selected projects include next-generation battery solutions, robotic systems with sensing capabilities for the extreme lunar environment, and tools to prepare for construction of critical infrastructure, such as lunar landing pads.
NASA’s SBIR/STTR program provides support for entrepreneurs, startups, and small businesses to advance and commercialize technologies that can advance the agency’s missions.
Working with the program, a company’s path toward commercialization or infusion into NASA missions occurs in phases.
The latest awards involved two of these phases.
The new Phase I contracts will receive up to $225,000 each to establish the merit and feasibility of their proposed innovation.
A portion of the projects selected are STTR awards, provided to small businesses partnered with research institutions.

The Phase II awards, with 98 contracts valued at up to $1.3 million each, will continue work begun in Phase I projects selected in 2025, targeting demonstration and delivery of the innovative technologies.
Following are a few examples of research supported through these recent awards:

An SBIR Phase II award for Opterus Research and Development Inc. supports a project focused on bringing power to the surface of the Moon and Mars by developing a modular system of rollable solar arrays.
The arrays can be handled robotically, are compatible with various support structures, and work even in dusty surface conditions.
The technology could be scaled up to 50 kilowatts, and it could provide a reliable power source to help both NASA and commercial space companies develop infrastructure on the Moon .
This SBIR Phase I award, led by Intelligent Fiber Optic Systems Corporation, aims to help lunar rovers perform complex tasks independently on the Moon.
The firm’s 10-foot, extendable robotic arm can both “see” and has a sense of touch, combining a camera with sensors to detect and measure surface textures, contact forces, and temperature.
The technology could help automate many lunar surface tasks, such as cleaning solar panels, positioning habitat structures, and collecting scientific samples from hard-to-reach locations.
On Earth, the same instrumented robotic arms could be used to inspect and repair power lines, nuclear reactors, or other infrastructure in hazardous environments.
Elementium Materials Inc., selected for an SBIR Phase I award, is developing an ultra-cold-tolerant battery module for space applications and cold-climate uses on Earth.
The technology can operate down to minus 76 degrees Fahrenheit without active heating, reducing the need for heaters and insulating layers to work on the Moon.
With the space and mass that’s saved, NASA missions can launch other tools and science experiments, instead.
This battery technology could help keep rovers, habitats, and other infrastructure running through the frigid, 14-day lunar night and potentially on Mars.

A collaboration between Slate Geotechnical Consultants Inc. and the Colorado School of Mines will evaluate two approaches to preparing lunar regolith for repeated lunar landings, so that routine mission activities can have sturdy, reusable landing pads.

Without such pads, the force generated by a rocket can blast out loose, gravel-like regolith from the surface, throw up dust, or create craters, potentially damaging spacecraft and nearby infrastructure.
The project, supported by an STTR Phase I award, will also investigate ways to use rovers to repair and maintain future lunar landing pads.
Complete lists of the selected proposals are available on the SBIR/STTR program’s website:

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
paras: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel.
A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers).
The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.

Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.
“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler.

The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington.
“But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”
Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space.
Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum.
A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1.
For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).
Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth.
Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone.
They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.
Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment.

Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons.
Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus.
Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.
“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director.

“Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space.
As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

In addition to their suite of scientific instruments , the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record , a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.
“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration.

Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech.
“Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit.
We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”

Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere , the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space.
Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018.
“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL.
“One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1.
Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin?
Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”

Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft.

Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator .
Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity.
With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year.

The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer.

As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network , large antennas located at three facilities around the world.
“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly.
It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL.
“Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us.
One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”

articles.title: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars
paras: An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before.
This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects.
A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.
A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse.

Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe.
To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky.
Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

“We don’t see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can’t just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from,” said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany.
“We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it.
There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”
Traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world.
Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.
Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points.
This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers .
The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.
“We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data,” Gazith said.
Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores.
Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.
The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star.

These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

“We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn’t find,” said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study.

“The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”
The discovery would not have happened without NASA’s longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone.
Launched in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light.
After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.
“The nice thing about NASA data is it’s all open,” Clark said.
“All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.”
That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset.
NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA’s Fermitools , enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.
The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with new findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

“Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search,” said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
“It’s made all of the science better.”

articles.title: MAF EAP – Holidays – How to manage the BAH HUMBUG that tries to sneak in
paras: Holidays are often a fun break during a busy year – a long weekend here and there is an event many of us can get behind.
However, when a short holiday break turns into a full holiday season, we know that this is a different “ball game”.
Everyone has stress about something – some people love the holidays, and some people are holiday-avoidant… and some live in the middle.
What specific stressors or challenges you experience might not bother your sibling, your spouse or your coworker.
We want to be aware of and have a clear understanding of what holidays mean to you as a person.

The first step is to acknowledge what your feelings and emotions are – you may enjoy seeing the neighborhood holiday lights but not want to decorate yourself (totally okay!!), you may love shopping for the perfect gift for everyone on your list, you may avoid all of the activities — everyone one of these is an okay choice… you can be yourself always in all ways.
Give yourself that permission.
As you prepare, keep a list or a calendar of events – expected/obligated, okay to go or not go,
Combine this with your standard calendar and make a schedule.
If you want, add to the list what your part is (bring a dish, gift, coordinate a visit, etc.).
Having the majority of activities written down will help you not overbook, help you plan ahead, make it easier to say no, spend within your budget.
Before you commit to something, say “I have to check my calendar first….
I will get back to you”.
Prepare your budget – We often budget for gifts but forget that we will be buying more groceries for those special meals and favorite dishes….
We also need to budget for travel, having guests in your home, clothing, even allow for a higher electric bill.
Write it down – keep receipts – let your immediate family know that this is what we have to spend, then track it as you go.
Now that you have a current calendar and a working budget, set realistic expectations for your holiday experience.
We know that not everything is optional and traditions will continue but none of it has to be perfect…minor stress and family friction can be normal.
When telling someone no, use “I” statements and stick to the single issue at hand.
In addition to your list/calendar, remember to prioritize time for yourself.
Keep your regular sleep schedule as much as possible, eat well (if you have a heavy meal one day, lighten up the next), schedule time to get fresh air and a quick break.
ALWAYS focus on what matters.
Focus on meaningful connections rather than activities that cause you anxiety.
If you feel emotional, take a few moments alone and identify the feeling, honor yourself for being able to face it and breathe through it (avoid pushing it down).
Remember how many times you have gotten through a “pressure moment” and give yourself credit.
Call a trusted friend or your therapist if you feel overwhelmed for longer than a day….and, please call 988 if you feel overwhelmed to an extreme. 988 is always available and waiting to help.
Look for the glimmers – find a happy moment (no matter how brief), find the memories that make you smile.
Thinking of something joyful changes your emotional state… train yourself to do this any time you need a lift.

Ultimately, we want to move away from focusing on the future (It causes anxiety) or overthinking about the past (it causes depression) ….and find yourself in the here and now where you have power to manage things happening around you.
Your power is with you in the present.
(Eckert Tolle book – The Power of Now).
The holiday season lasts for weeks – gift yourself with
With the extra pressure of the holiday season, our feelings can often be stronger than other times during the year…. if you start having feelings:
Anxious – take deep breaths, focus ONLY on the present – your surroundings, what you see, count objects, put ice on the inside of your wrists (this works really well!)
Angry – walk away for a moment, take a break, give yourself as long as you need to regulate these feelings, know that whoever gets angry first loses…be the winner in the moment.
Helpless, hopeless, trapped (discouraged) – remember that you have a voice, it is sometimes difficult to use it in family situations, but you can talk to yourself.
Remember how strong you are, how many accomplishments you have completed…. reframe the situation so you recall all of your wonderful qualities.
Overwhelmed – Check your list/holiday calendar again…what can you change or take off the list.
What can you postpone for 24-48 hours?
What can you give someone else to do?
What can you order from the store rather than do the cooking or shopping yourself?
Find a quick solution for one or two things (at least) and take some pressure off.
Grief – acknowledge how you feel, we do not have to be cheerful just because it is a holiday.
Say no to any event or activity that feels too “heavy” and give yourself permission to leave if it becomes too much.
Find a way to keep their memory with you – carry a favorite picture or memento.
Find a grief support group.
Basically, we want to notice the small things and find gratitude in what we have.
Our outward situation does not define us.
If you find that holiday time is difficult or stressful, always give yourself permission to contact your EAP services for assistance and support.

articles.title: NASA Announces Mid-Power Electric Rocket Challenge for US Companies
paras: NASA launched a new competition inviting U.S. companies to produce prototypes of mid-power Hall effect thrusters – a type of electric propulsion system considered crucial for future space operations and exploration.
Hall effect thrusters use an electric field to accelerate a propellant gas, producing efficient thrust for long-duration missions.
Used for propelling satellites and deep space robotic vehicles, Hall effect thruster systems are critical technology.

NASA’s Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket (AMPERE) Challenge is offering $500,000, split between two winning U.S. companies, to accelerate the maturation of mid-power systems that could be foundational to supporting future NASA and commercial missions.
Interested parties can learn more at an AMPERE Virtual Industry Day hosted by NASA on Thursday, Nov. 19.

“This challenge approach seeks to remove key barriers and facilitate commercialization by providing access to NASA subject matter expertise, state-of-the-art technologies, and world-class facilities at no cost to challenge winners,” said Dr. Jason Frieman, AMPERE project co-owner at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.
“We hope participants will see this as an opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities to NASA and other government and commercial stakeholders.”

The competition is the first of NASA’s Tech Maturation Prize series, which seeks to accelerate development of breakthrough technologies in support of NASA missions while strengthening the U.S. space economy.
The competition includes three phases.
In Phase 1, each participating team will submit a concept design, manufacturing plan, and cost and performance projections.
NASA may select two winners to advance to Phase 2, where teams will develop prototypes and collaborate with NASA personnel.
Through no-cost licensing, these teams can gain early access to NASA-developed Hall effect thruster technologies that use krypton as a propellant.
In Phase 3, prototypes will be tested at NASA Glenn at no cost to the participating teams.
In total, two winning teams may be selected to receive up to $250,000 each.
The AMPERE Challenge is open for registration until Jan. 27, 2027, at 5 p.m. EST.
The challenge supports the Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket project, managed by NASA Glenn and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
The project is funded by the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate .

articles.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
paras: NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17.

The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision.
Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own.
Submissions are due March 1, 2027.
Every mission requires a power source.
Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions.
Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight.
“As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible.

Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington.
“NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design.
We cannot wait to see what they come up with!”
Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration.
Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission.

Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable.
Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12.
One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions.

Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space.
NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country.
U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website .

The Power to Explore Student Challenge is funded by the NASA Science Mission Directorate and operates out of the Radioisotope Power Systems Program under the Research and Technology Mission Directorate.
Future Engineers administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

articles.title: BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge
paras: The NASA Space Biology Program within the Biological and Physical Sciences (BPS) Division investigates how living systems respond across the full spectrum of biological organization to advance understanding of how living systems respond to the unique stressors of space exploration—including microgravity, ionizing radiation, low magnetic fields, and elevated CO₂.
As NASA prepares for long-duration deep space missions, the need to protect individual crew members with personalized, data-driven health strategies is becoming increasingly important.

The original AVATAR (A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response) investigation, which flew aboard the Artemis II mission, marks a significant milestone: organ-on-a-chip devices constructed from the cells of actual crew members returned from a 10-day lunar flyby on April 10, 2026.

AVATAR is the first demonstration of an Artemis astronaut analog using an organ-on-a-chip model to generate personalized biological insights that can inform medical kits and countermeasures for future deep space missions.
Digital twins represent a key strategy for addressing these challenges.
By developing individualized computational physiological models that can be iteratively refined with empirical data, these frameworks integrate environmental, physiological, and multi-omics inputs.
This approach allows for the simulation and prediction of how a specific individual will respond to spaceflight stressors.

The BPS Digital AVATAR Challenge invites the scientific community to apply innovative computational digital twin technologies to accelerate biological discovery, biochemical and molecular modeling, and predictions of individual astronaut health outcomes.
The digital twin will be a computational model of how the AVATAR bone marrow chip responds to spaceflight stressors.

The proposed digital twin frameworks must be capable of processing diverse multi-modal datasets and leverage established computational biology methods alongside modern digital twin architectures to create personalized, predictive models of astronaut physiology.

These systems are expected to model each astronaut’s immune and bone marrow hematopoietic responses to spaceflight, integrating multi-modal data to generate tailored health predictions — including comparative analysis that distinguishes individual-specific effects from effects common across the crew.
Proposals should also demonstrate a pathway to continuous model updating as new empirical data become available, reflecting the iterative nature of a true digital twin.
For more information including registration , rules, and eligibility, visit: https://work.crowdplat.com/challenge/bps-digital-twin-challenge

articles.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge Breaks Global Hackathon Records
paras: On Nov. 14 and 15, NASA held the annual Space Apps Challenge with a record-breaking 181,835 registered participants taking part in 593 events around the world.
The annual hackathon invites participants to use NASA’s open data to address one of 14 challenges focused on space exploration or Earth science.
This year, the hackathon drew 59% more registrants and was the 5th year in a row with increased participation.
Since 2012, NASA Space Apps Challenge has hosted the two-day event, which has included more than 600,000 people from more than 190 countries.

articles.title: Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read
Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University

During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area.
These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated.
Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate.
Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.
Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems.
As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life.
Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils.
Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?

When Perseverance previously encountered silica-rich rocks on the inner rim of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential.
Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.

articles.title: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
paras: Astronauts James A.
Lovell Jr. and Edwin E.
“Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.

In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space.
The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface.

One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T.

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet.

articles.title: A Global Rebound for Mangroves
paras: Scientists began using satellites to map mangrove forests in the 1970s after the launch of the first Landsat satellite.
For decades, the story they told about mangroves was dominated by loss and decline.
Research published in Science suggests that the tide has turned.
A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America.
The researchers analyzed Landsat imagery collected between 1984 and 2023, looking for signs of changes in the extent and density of mangrove canopy.

They tallied losses of nearly 3,000 square kilometers (1,200 square miles) between 1984 and 2010, followed by an unexpected increase of nearly 2,000 square kilometers (770 square miles) of mangroves after 2010.
They also found that many of today’s mangrove forests have denser, more closed canopies than they did in 2010, a sign of healthier, less degraded forests, particularly in South America.

“Other research groups have mapped and analyzed long-term changes in select regions, but these are the first global mangrove maps that cover such a long period,” said Zhen Zhang, an environmental scientist at Tulane University.
“About two-thirds of the expansion was due to mangroves colonizing new areas and the other third due to restoration and regrowth in degraded areas,” he added.
One of the most notable reversals occurred in Southeast Asia—especially Burma (Myanmar).

The country lost mangroves rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s due to the expansion of agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting in coastal areas, but the trend reversed around 2010, when mangrove area began expanding in many places.

The authors attribute the turnaround to increased awareness and restoration efforts after the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004 , strengthened legal protections for forests, and high rates of sedimentation that opened up new mudflats for colonization.

The pair of Landsat images above shows expansion of mangrove forests in Palaw Township in Burma’s Myeik District—an area that has seen both significant regeneration of degraded mangrove forests and the spread of trees into new areas since 2010.
In this region, much of the regeneration appears to be occurring in abandoned rice fields (brown) south of the village of Kyauktaung.
People on nearby Pyin Bukyi Island, meanwhile, have experimented with conservation projects and tree planting efforts to support mangroves.
Despite the gains, deforestation remains a common challenge in Burma, which lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010.
Since then, the country’s mangrove area has grown about 10 percent.

Mangrove trees are relatively small—averaging about 13 meters (43 feet)—but mighty from an ecological perspective, with mangrove ecosystems storing up to four times as much carbon as taller inland tropical forests.

The trees play an important role in protecting coastal communities from erosion and storm surges, and their distinctive stilt-like roots provide habitat and vital nursery grounds for fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine life.

In several areas, such as around the mouth of the Amazon River and in northern Australia, extensive deposition of sediment has created new mudflats that mangroves have successfully colonized, contributing to steady increases in each of these regions since the 1990s.

At the northern and southern edges of their range, including the southeastern U.S., warming temperatures and fewer freezes have also allowed mangroves to push into areas that were previously too cold, Zhang explained.
There are some areas, however, where losses have outweighed gains.
Substantial mangrove losses in the Niger Delta, for instance, have reduced the total mangrove area in West and Central Africa since 2010.
North America and southern Africa, meanwhile, have seen widespread degradation after tropical cyclones devastated broad swaths of mangroves.
“The global successes we’ve seen with mangroves during the past decade should not be seen as grounds for complacency,” cautioned Zhang.
“This underscores that conservation and slowing deforestation can lead to huge positive impacts when coupled with natural expansion and regeneration.”

articles.title: NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman
paras: Science Observatory Team Multimedia News More 5 min read

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object.
The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter.
Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.
Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects.
Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe.
While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view.
If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble’s high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter.

Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses.
In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.
By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images.
The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.
The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models.
Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs.
The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy.
Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy.
Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.
Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red.
These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars.
Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.
Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact.
Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.
But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies.
In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.
Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing.
The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring.
Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.
These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak.
Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations.
Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos.

As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

articles.title: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
paras: For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA.

Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history.
Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander.

The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028.
Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives.
“I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said.
“In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details.
How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails?
Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity?
Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft?
And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems?
Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.”
Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture.
After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children.
She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory , performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists.

“I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said.
From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station.

She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed.
It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations.
Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018.
The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her.
Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications.
“Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said.
“On my own, I studied engineering principles.
I passed boards and certification tests.
I learned to speak ‘engineer!’”
Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight.
Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface.

“I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said.
As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before.

In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.
