articles.title: Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA
paras: As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission.

These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time.
Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers.

“Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California.
“I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video.
It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.”

Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey.
Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images.
“The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer.
“People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover.
We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.”
Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride.
After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight.
Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats.

Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.
“The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to plan the shots,” Thomas said.
“I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters.
We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles.
Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these issues in the planning process.”

The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier.
Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions.

The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

articles.title: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir
paras: Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S.
Southwest in late October and early November 2026.
The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods.
One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir.
The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 .
In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S.
Army Corps of Engineers.
(Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.)
On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date.
That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity.
Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels.
The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather.
Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding.
In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage .
After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood .
Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property.
Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks.

From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026.
Though the downpours posed hazards to communities along many rivers, they did provide drought relief throughout the region.
Weekly U.S.
Drought Monitor maps, derived from a suite of satellite data products and ground-based observations, have indicated improvements to drought conditions due to the fall storms.
The group’s November 3 summary noted that “short-term drought has ended for the Southwest and Great Basin,” although long-term drought persists in places.
Wet weather in the Southwest is often associated with El Niño events, when the segment of the jet stream flowing eastward near the equatorial Pacific tends to strengthen.
Experts noted that the low-pressure system delivering the heavy rainfall in autumn 2026 was at a low latitude for the time of year and drew energy from unusually high ocean temperatures.
El Niño patterns—like the one currently underway —can increase the likelihood of moisture-laden storms being steered across the Southwest interior.

articles.title: Autumn Mornings Bring Valley Fog
paras: On a cool November morning, low clouds traced the branching valleys of the Appalachian Plateau and the Cumberland River.
By afternoon, they had faded, leaving clear skies over the autumn landscape.
The change is visible in this pair of images from November 8, 2026.
The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite acquired the left image that morning.
In this natural-color view, low clouds appear white as they fill many of the valleys.
Autumn vegetation appears in shades of brown and green.
The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on NOAA-21 acquired the right image that afternoon, after the clouds had dissipated and exposed the rivers and lakes beneath them.
This false-color view makes it easier to distinguish water (dark blue) from vegetation (bright green).
The clouds appear to be fog, a type of cloud that forms near the ground .
Foggy mornings in the region are common this time of year.

As nights lengthen, the ground has more time to radiate away the day’s heat, and the air just above it cools to the dew point —the temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapor begins condensing into the tiny droplets that make up fog.
Because cold air is denser than warm air, it flows downslope and pools in valleys, so fog tends to form there first.
Notice the fog filling the branching valleys across part of the Appalachian Plateau in eastern Kentucky and southwestern West Virginia.
Rivers and streams that run along many of the valley floors add to the effect by supplying extra moisture.
The same pattern is visible along the Cumberland River and its reservoirs in north-central Tennessee and south-central Kentucky.
According to the National Weather Service, temperatures in many places on the morning of November 8 dipped into the 30s Fahrenheit before giving way to a mild, sunny afternoon.
Forecasters reported locally dense valley fog that morning.
Dense fog had also blanketed a wider part of the region earlier in the week, prompting advisories for hazardous travel conditions.

articles.title: NASA to Welcome Expedition 74 Astronauts Home at Space Center Houston
paras: NASA will welcome home the Expedition 74 crew during a public event at Space Center Houston following their return from a long-duration mission aboard the International Space Station.

NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams; ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Sophie Adenot; and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud‑Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev will share mission highlights at 6 p.m. CST Tuesday, Nov. 17, at NASA Johnson Space Center’s visitor center.
An awards ceremony recognizing key mission contributors will follow the presentation.
The astronauts will be available for media interviews before the event.
Media may request an in-person interview no later than 5 p.m. Monday, Nov. 16, by emailing the JSC Newsroom at jsc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov .
Williams, Kud‑Sverchkov, and Mikaev launched aboard the Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on Nov. 27, 2025.
The trio returned to Earth on July 26, making a parachute-assisted landing southeast of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan.
The crew was in space for 241 days, orbiting the Earth 3,856 times and traveling more than 102 million miles.
The mission was the first for Williams and Mikaev and the second for Kud-Sverchkov.
Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot launched aboard a Dragon spacecraft on Feb. 13 as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
After more than seven months aboard the space station, Meir, Hathaway, and Adenot safely splashed down on Oct. 8 in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles.
During their 237-day mission, the four crew members traveled more than 100 million miles and completed more than 3,792 orbits around Earth.
The mission was the second for Meir and the first for Hathaway and Adenot.
Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev also flew as part of Crew-12 but is unavailable for the event.
The Expedition 74 crew dedicated more than 1,400 hours to scientific research and technology demonstrations aboard the International Space Station.
Its work advanced in-space manufacturing by testing metal and tissue 3D-printing technologies and supported human health studies examining the effects of long-duration spaceflight.
Research included blood flow studies, assessments of piloting capabilities under changing gravitational conditions, and activation of a new compact exercise system .
The crew also evaluated life-support and environmental systems critical to future exploration missions under NASA’s Artemis program.
In addition, the crew members conducted pharmaceutical research to crystalize proteins for cancer medications , advance tumor targeting treatments , and grow stem cells for therapeutics.

They cared for the first set of plants studied outside of curated systems , upgraded an instrument used to advance our understanding of matter and develop new quantum technologies, managed visiting spacecraft, and performed essential maintenance to support the continued operation of the orbiting laboratory.

Beyond research and operational achievements, Expedition 74 engaged students and audiences around the world through live educational events, outreach activities, and the sharing of stunning imagery that highlights the importance of scientific discovery and international collaboration in space.
For more than 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs not possible on Earth.

The space station helps NASA understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and to Mars.

articles.title: NASA Scientists Show How Gravitational Waves Can Reveal New Worlds
paras: The LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna) observatory, now in development, will detect gravitational waves, the tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses.
Now two studies led by NASA astrophysicists show in new detail how LISA could reveal a new and unique population of exoplanets — worlds beyond our solar system — throughout our galaxy.

“The most common source for LISA is expected to be double white dwarf systems, which are binaries composed of white dwarfs in tight orbits,” said Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
“If an exoplanet also orbits within one of these systems, its presence becomes imprinted on the gravitational wave signal in a way we’ll be able to uncover.”
Two papers published Tuesday in The Astrophysical Journal detail the findings.
The first , authored solely by McGrath, examines the detection method and determines the planet masses and orbital periods where it would work best.
The second paper , by McGrath and coauthors, investigates how such planets could be confirmed using NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope .
The possibility of detecting exoplanets around LISA double white dwarf systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008.
Led by ESA (European Space Agency), the LISA mission is slated for launch in the mid-2030s.
As a collaborative partner, NASA is contributing the telescopes, other critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support as part of its mission to better understand how the universe works.
The LISA detection method is similar to one called radial velocity that uses light and is already employed to find exoplanets around nearby stars.
As a planet orbits, its gravity tugs on its host star, imparting a small reflex motion, or wobble, onto it.
This wobble causes the star’s spectrum to oscillate, with spectral lines shifting from redder wavelengths as the star moves away from us to bluer ones as the star moves toward us.
The shift is due to a phenomenon called the Doppler effect .
“Something similar occurs with gravitational waves,” said Scott Noble, a theoretical astrophysicist at NASA Goddard and a coauthor on the confirmation paper.
“By themselves, double white dwarfs will emit gravitational waves at a nearly continuous frequency.
Add a sufficiently massive planet to the system, and its presence causes the binary to experience reflex motion, adding a Doppler modulation to the gravitational signal.”
For LISA, this modulation will appear as sidebands, secondary signals at both higher and lower frequencies than the primary one.

McGrath likens the situation to modern radio communication, where some of the energy of a main radio carrier frequency goes into forming sidebands at adjacent upper and lower frequencies that carry messages (like voices or music).
For gravitational waves, the sidebands carry messages about the presence of a planet.
White dwarfs are the Earth-sized remnants of stars like the Sun.

While exoplanets have been detected around a few isolated white dwarfs, none have yet been found around a binary white dwarf, which means the LISA detections would represent a distinct new exoplanet population.

Astronomers estimate that our Milky Way galaxy contains 10 million double white dwarf systems with orbital periods of less than an hour, which generate gravitational waves in the right range for LISA to find.
They expect LISA will resolve about 10,000 individual systems, as well as around 100 mixed binaries — with white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes — orbiting in similar periods.

“Once LISA captures its first exoplanet detections, it will be critical for us to validate some of them,” said Mary Anne Limbach, an assistant research scientist at the University of Michigan and a co-author on the confirmation paper.
“These joint detections will allow us to establish that the gravitational signals correspond to genuine planets rather than false positives.”
The team described a new method for confirming these planets by taking advantage of the Webb telescope’s infrared sensitivity.
A planet in a double white dwarf system produces a larger portion of infrared light than what’s expected from the stars themselves.
Webb’s instruments can easily detect this infrared excess out to a distance of at least 500 light-years.

Using this technique for a test case system at this distance, the researchers find that Webb could detect an exoplanet about five times Jupiter’s mass, while LISA could detect a sub-Jupiter exoplanet under ideal circumstances.
The LISA observatory will consist of a trio of spacecraft following Earth as it orbits the Sun.
They will form a vast triangular array stretching 1.6 million miles (2.5 million kilometers) on each side.
Each spacecraft will include two telescopes that will use infrared laser beams to simultaneously transmit and receive signals between adjacent spacecraft.
Through these telescopes, the spacecraft will measure miniscule changes — smaller than the width of a helium atom — in their relative distances, the signals of passing gravitational waves.
Gravitational waves were predicted by Albert Einstein’s 1916 general theory of relativity and first detected by ground-based observatories in 2015 .
The waves form whenever massive objects accelerate, such as two stars in orbit around each other.
They travel through space-time, moving at the speed of light, and are unaffected by objects they encounter along the way.
These properties make them a valuable tool for probing the cosmos.

Additional NASA contributions to the mission include the laser system, devices to manage the buildup of electric charge on the proof masses, data analysis for identifying and characterizing individual gravitational wave sources, and additional scientific and engineering expertise.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5056-5062: Charging Back Up!
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home 3 min read
Today’s plan covered 3 sols, 5060, 5061, and 5062, as we take a few recharging sols before getting back to our normal drilling activities.
As you may know if you have been following the blog closely, we are in the middle of a drilling campaign on our target called “Nazca.”

We’ve already drilled the hole, characterized the tailings from the drill hole with ChemCam, and have now done several sample dropoffs, both to our SAM and CheMin instruments within the belly of the rover.
We still have a number of activities left to do as part of the campaign, including another dropoff to SAM for a different kind of analysis, and drilling cleanup activities.
One of those activities is called “RAGE” (Rotate to Agitate for Granule Expulsion, a very fun acronym) where we essentially shake the drill to get any remaining sample out of it.
We’ll also make sure to take lots of imaging to continue document the drill hole and tailings.
In any case, those activities are very power-hungry for our rover!
So today’s plan purposefully did not have a lot of activities in it so we could get a nice few power positive sols before we get back to drilling.
Each of our three sols had a standard morning science block, with an extra exciting brand-new activity on 5061 (more on that shortly!).

Over the three sols, we conducted remote science with ChemCam active and Remote Micro-Imager mosaics on some interesting targets (“Titicaca,” “Pampas,” and “Salta”), some Mastcam imaging of our calibration target and our drill target, several Navcam dust devil studies and Mastcam tau observations, and twilight imaging.
Despite this plan being recharging/waiting, we got in lots of exciting science to continue to study the Nazca crystal formations and the nearby layered rocks and bedrock.
On 5061, we also conducted a brand-new engineering activity to test parallelism over one of our downlink communications windows.
As the rover gets older and our power output slowly decreases over the length of the mission, we are continuously looking for new ways to execute activities with less power use.
One of our strategies is parallelism – having two activities execute at the same time will save power due to the rover being awake for less time.
However, we need to vet pairs of activities ahead of time to ensure they are safe to run together.
This is a test of one of those pairs – running our CheMin “Get Data” activity at the same time as we are sending data to one of our orbiters.
CheMin Get Data is a high CPU activity which transfers science data from the instrument to our flight computers.
The test seems to have gone well, but we’ll have to wait to hear back from our engineering team to analyze the results!
Overall, it was an exciting plan full of great remote science as we wait to be able to wrap up our drill campaign.
Stay tuned to hear more about how the rest of the Nazca campaign went!

articles.title: Rubies on Mars?
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home Written by Roger C.
Wiens, SuperCam Principal Investigator for NASA’s Perseverance rover at Purdue University
Exploration on Mars turns up the unexpected.
Perseverance is equipped with a fantastic set of instruments for studying the rock record of this ancient planet.
Both PIXL and SuperCam have great capabilities for detecting all kinds of elements.
SHERLOC, SuperCam, and PIXL can detect minerals using various techniques including x-ray fluorescence, Raman, and infrared spectroscopies.
As a side benefit of the way SuperCam performs its Raman spectroscopy, it can also study time-resolved luminescence.
Normally luminescence occurs over a broad wavelength range (most of Earth’s commercial lighting uses luminescence in some way or another).
Two years ago, the SuperCam team was startled to find strong, narrow luminescence peaks at two wavelengths of 692.7 and 694.1 nanometers when they shot a light-colored rock with the laser.
This luminescence comes from delayed atomic transitions in chromium atoms present in a corundum mineral structure.
SuperCam can time the delay of the atomic transitions via the resulting photons, and so we could verify that this emission came from chromium in corundum.
The results were published in Geophysical Research Letters by a team led by Ann Ollila earlier this year, so you can read all about it.
The gemstone version of chromium-containing corundum is ruby.
Prior to installing SuperCam on Perseverance, we placed a ruby in the laser beam and watched the entire room pulse a brilliant red as SuperCam’s laser beam hit the gemstone; it was extremely bright.
While we haven’t found collectable rubies on Mars yet, the little corundum crystals are helping us learn more about Mars’ past.
Corundum is a metamorphic and pegmatitic mineral which we would not expect to find on Mars, a planet that lacks plate tectonics.
However, large meteor and asteroid impacts can create local metamorphism due to long-term heating from the impact.
Because we are in a very ancient terrain near the rim of Jezero crater, we can expect some evidence of localized metamorphism.
As the first mission in such terrain, we are learning new things.

Earlier in the mission we tried this technique only rarely; lately we have carried out the time-resolved luminescence observations frequently on light-toned rocks to look for more evidence of impact effects.
It’s great to have this unexpected tool on board as we delve further into Mars’ deep past.

articles.title: NASA Announces $1 Million to Students for Moon Base Challenge
paras: On Sunday, NASA announced the opening of its $1 million Moon Base Student Challenge during a MAX POWER event at Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex in Florida.
As part of a Golden Age of Science, the competition invites student teams at U.S. high schools and post-secondary schools to contribute designs for the Moon Base.
“We’re looking for students ready to think creatively, work as a team, and take on real problems connected to NASA’s future on the Moon,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“You do not have to wait until graduation to contribute.
Curiosity, creativity, and the willingness to tackle hard problems without obvious answers are exactly the qualities we need as we build what comes next.”
NASA is building a Moon Base where astronauts will live, work, and explore at the lunar South Pole region.
A permanent human presence on the Moon paves the way for future crewed missions to Mars and requires talent from various industries and backgrounds.

“As we build and design the foundations of Moon Base, we want to leverage all the ingenuity and innovation to think of every consideration our explorers might need to live and work there,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program.
“Students bring exactly the bold ideas that we’re looking for, and I’m looking forward to their fresh perspective.
Ultimately, Moon Base is for them, people who will experience a world where humans are on the Moon to stay.”
The multiphase challenge supports NASA’s commitment to cultivating the technical skills of tomorrow’s aerospace workforce.

For this challenge, student teams will design innovative solutions for Moon Base across six categories: power generation and storage, construction, life-support systems, surface mobility, communications networks, and astronaut safety.
The challenge gives participants an opportunity to develop necessary skills for careers in the space industry while helping advance new concepts for Moon Base technologies.
Participants are required to register for the challenge through the NASA STEM Gateway.
Registration is open until Jan. 25, 2027.
“Students are the next generation of explorers and innovators.

Their unique perspectives are key to helping us envision a future away from Earth, and I’m excited to see the creativity and ingenuity spurred by this challenge,” said Elaine Ho, associate administrator for the Office of STEM Engagement at NASA Headquarters.
The Moon Base Student Challenge addresses authentic environmental and mission design parameters for life and operations on the lunar surface.

The deliverables reflect industry skills – such as trade studies, concept proposals, and stakeholder briefings – allowing participants across technical, vocational, and various academic tracks to build career-relevant skills without requiring prior specialized engineering or technical experience.
The Office of STEM Engagement designed the challenge in collaboration with the Moon Base Program.

The Institute of Competition Sciences administers the challenge through a contract with the NASA Center of Excellence for Collaborative Innovation within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.

articles.title: NASA Awards Moon Base Transportation, Technology, Science Projects
paras: NASA announced a suite of awards and mission updates on Saturday to expand the agency’s Moon Base exploration, science, and infrastructure capabilities.

The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.
The agency shared the news at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get more better and more capable with every mission.
When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”

“In the eight months since Ignition, we’ve made incredible strides in accomplishing the near impossible: establishing a permanent outpost on the lunar surface,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager, Moon Base Program.

“We’ve consolidated numerous efforts into a streamlined program, evolving our human exploration architecture into an iterative and sustained campaign for Moon Base technology development and implementation.
Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.”
To strengthen the cargo lander network needed to support the Moon Base, NASA selected eight companies for the next phase of its CLPS ( Commercial Lunar Payload Services ) initiative.
The companies are eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under the new CLPS 2 contract:

Under the CLPS 2 framework, the companies will provide lunar delivery services, including managing, building, and operating landers that transport NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads to the Moon.
The CLPS 2 framework is a 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract with a combined maximum value of $10 billion.
NASA increased the value of the current CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives.
The original CLPS contract will remain in place through November 2028, with an additional five-year period to complete awarded lunar deliveries through November 2033.
NASA also announced it is moving forward with development of PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration) .

Carrying science instruments and technology demonstrations, the six-wheeled rover will land at the Moon’s South Pole to characterize the surface and subsurface, assess resource potential, and provide data to enable landing site selection, as well as future infrastructure and exploration activities.
The nuclear-powered rover can operate during long lunar nights and within permanently shadowed regions thought to harbor ice, which is crucial for a sustained human presence on the Moon.

The agency’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, a division of Caltech, will manage the mission and build the rover from a combination of spare flight components and engineering test models for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers.
Using proven hardware, software, and Mars rover operation approaches significantly reduces cost and enables integration and testing of the complex PROMISE rover on a shorter timeline.
NASA has assessed the compatibility of the hardware with the lunar environment and determined it can tolerate the harsh conditions found near the Moon’s South Pole.

The PROMISE rover will carry a drill to extract regolith, or lunar dust, to characterize ice and other resources from approximately 3 feet (1 meter) below the surface, spectrometers for analyzing the chemical composition of surface material, temperature and radiation sensors, and visible-light cameras.
It will demonstrate a next-generation, radiation-tolerant computing system, NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing , and advanced autonomy sensors and algorithms.
NASA is targeting late 2028 to launch PROMISE and planning an 18-month mission for the rover.
NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, with an option period worth an additional $140 million based on performance to deliver PROMISE to the lunar South Pole.
The award expands the task order awarded in May 2026 to deliver two lunar terrain vehicles to the Moon.
Blue Origin will use its Mark 1 lander to deliver and deploy the rover as part of the Moon Base’s first phase.
Delivering Moon Base infrastructure will require a robust transportation network between Earth and the Moon.
Orbital Transfer Vehicles (OTVs) act like long-distance freight trucks, carrying large loads across space.
Lunar landers handle the final delivery, bringing supplies, equipment, and infrastructure safely down to the Moon’s surface.
To demonstrate those capabilities, NASA awarded six task orders as part of the agency’s Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) launch services contract.
The awards were given to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin, and Impulse Space to integrate and transport Moon Base cargo.
Three mission types will allow NASA flexibility to fly science and technology demonstrations when they are ready.
The first will include missions to reduce risks of future long-term human spaceflight for lunar exploration.

The missions will verify that communication and navigation methods work properly during the journey from Earth orbit to the Moon, and OTV capability to support delivery of a CLPS lunar lander to a desired orbit.
This mission type will deliver the CAPSTONE 02 spacecraft to deep space to test proximity maneuvers, navigation, and communications around the Moon.

The second category of missions will prepare the lunar South Pole for human exploration by sending a group of highly mobile drones to survey the surface before astronauts arrive, enabling safer, more informed human missions while demonstrating advanced robotic capabilities.

Such missions will include the agency’s MoonFall drones, designed to scout areas beyond the reach of traditional rovers, as well as delivery of additional Moon Base assets necessary to support Phase One objectives.
To reduce risk for future missions, the third mission type will test navigation technologies and demonstrate operations in multiple cislunar orbits, between Earth and the Moon.
This mission type will demonstrate commercial orbital transfer capabilities intended to increase the amount of cargo that future landers can deliver to the lunar surface.

The task orders have a value of approximately $1.3 billion combined and fall under the 10-year VADR indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, which has a maximum total value of $5 billion across all contracts.
The VADR contracts are managed by NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center as part of the agency’s Commercial Access to Space Program.

By procuring multiple launch and in-space transportation services together, NASA provides industry with a more predictable set of mission opportunities while gaining access to a broader range of commercial capabilities for future lunar exploration.
Some missions will launch aboard Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R, and SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets.
In-space transportation spacecraft for these missions will be provided by Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Impulse Space, and Quantum Space.
Complementing those in-space transportation demonstrations, NASA selected SpaceX for the Cislunar Communications Deployment Demonstration under an existing lunar logistics contract.
Through a Specialized Delivery Mission task order, SpaceX will launch communications satellites aboard a Starship to cislunar space in 2028.
The demonstration will help inform the development of future lunar communications networks that keep astronauts, mission controllers, and the Moon Base connected.

To extend infrastructure capabilities on the lunar surface, NASA plans to purchase commercial components for a Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCAST), including solar arrays, batteries, and wireless power-transfer hardware.

The agency awarded Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, for energy storage capability, Redwire for power generation, and Yank Technologies, Inc., for wireless power transfer in support of miniCAST.
The miniCAST will combine power and communications capabilities to support future Moon Base activities.
Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, will assemble and test the systems before they are delivered to the lunar surface.
NASA expects work to begin within months, and the initial effort will involve components rather than a major integrated system.
The agency also plans a separate solicitation for fully integrated power systems, which is anticipated in early 2027.

NASA intends to release a directed call under its Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships, or NextSTEP-3 B, solicitation to help close architecture-driven , high-priority data gaps for Moon Base development.
The effort will help NASA gather information it needs to plan future missions, reduce risk, and support technologies and infrastructure for sustained operations on the Moon’s South Pole.
The work could include small spacecraft missions, payloads on future Moon Base flights, or the purchase of data collected by commercial partners.
As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before.

In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on this foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

articles.title: NASA Seeks Next Generation of Explorers to Join Astronaut Corps
paras: NASA is looking for the explorers who will help write the next chapter of human spaceflight.

Applications are now open for the agency’s next class of astronauts, who will join NASA as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base, and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars.

The next generation of astronauts will train to operate on the lunar surface, live and work beyond Earth, and take on missions that will push the boundaries of human exploration farther than ever before.
U.S. citizens interested in joining the astronaut corps have until 11:59 p.m. EST Thursday, Dec. 3, to submit their completed application materials at:
“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“The people we select could walk on the Moon, live and work at the Moon Base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars.
Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage.
NASA’s astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation.
If you are ready to join that tradition, come help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure.”
NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027 to begin training as the next class of astronaut candidates.
“The window is open.
The mission is waiting.
And the only thing missing from the greatest adventure humanity has ever embarked upon is you,” said NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson.
The agency last opened applications in 2024.
From more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are currently completing nearly two years of training.

“For those who apply, becoming a NASA astronaut is more than a career opportunity,” said Scott Tingle, chief astronaut and chair of the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.
“It is a chance to join a legacy of explorers who have pushed the boundaries of discovery and play a role in the missions that will shape humanity’s future in space.
The next generation of astronaut candidates could help write history while inspiring future scientists, engineers, and explorers.”
Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates for its increasingly challenging missions.
The agency has 32 astronauts active in the astronaut corps, and selected applicants will join their ranks to study spacewalking, lunar geology, operations of high-performance aircraft, and more.

articles.title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
paras: Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River.
In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment.
Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long, meandering path on its gradual journey downslope.
But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward.

Some experts think that within the later stages of this “ still-enigmatic ” history, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the San Juan’s headwaters , which increased the river’s gradient and sped its flow.
With that, the water’s erosive power intensified, and the river started carving its winding path deeper and deeper through 300-million-year-old rock.
Today, on its westward path to Lake Powell, the San Juan River flows through an impressive series of entrenched meanders, also known as “goosenecks.”
An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed the stark desert topography on October 6, 2026.
In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park , the river runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 meters) deep.
In places, it nearly loops back on itself, making horseshoe-shaped bends.
One section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 kilometers) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 kilometers) apart as the crow—nay, goose—flies.
While the goosenecks are an unusual geologic wonder to behold by day, the area’s dark skies are a spectacle by night.
Goosenecks State Park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021.

According to DarkSky International, features such as the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Messier 24 star cloud in the Sagittarius spiral arm of the Milky Way are visible to the unaided eye from the park.
In November 2026 , dark skies offer the chance to view several meteor showers, with the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids, and Leonids reaching their peaks throughout the month.
Astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830 was acquired on October 6, 2026, with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimeters.
It is provided by the ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit at NASA Johnson Space Center.
The image was taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew.
The image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed.

articles.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
paras: The island of Cyprus began to form some 90 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous , with molten rock pouring from the seafloor, solidifying, and building new oceanic crust .

Over time, portions of this oceanic rock were wrenched upward by tectonic forces , eventually emerging as a rugged island made of ophiolite , a type of rock with a mottled green appearance said to look like the skin of a snake.
Remnants of that ancient island are still visible in the dark rocks of the Troodos Mountains .

During the Miocene , considerably younger layers of chalk, limestone, marl, and other marine sedimentary rocks accumulated around the island, providing material that developed into a second, smaller island to the south during a later period of geologic uplift .
Over time, sediment poured from rivers into the channel separating the two islands and combined with marine sediments to create deltas and eventually two land bridges, or tombolos .
The joined landmass comprises the Akrotiri Peninsula , now the southernmost tip of Cyprus.
The sandy edges of the peninsula were visible when Landsat 8 captured these images on October 10, 2026.
Akrotiri Salt Lake , a coastal lagoon that was once an arm of the Mediterranean Sea, lies between the two tombolos.
The more westerly feature, the Kouris River tombolo, formed first, developing about 50,000 years ago from river-deposited gravels and sands.
The eastern tombolo extended southward from Cyprus, cutting off the Mediterranean Sea only within the past 2,000 years, according to geologists .
The lake’s water levels now vary markedly with the seasons, typically filling in the late autumn and winter and drying out in the summer.
The influx of winter water has historically attracted sizable overwintering flamingo populations, averaging about 4,000 birds.
However, the wintering flamingo population has declined in recent years, plummeting to 30 birds in 2025, according to news reports .
Flamingos have long flocked to the lake to feed on fairy shrimp , which are rich in colorful substances called carotenoids that give the birds their famously pink hue .
Snakes are another of the island’s more notorious animal inhabitants.
In antiquity, Cyprus was known as Ophiousa , or “ land of snakes ,” likely due to its robust population of blunt-nosed vipers .

According to legend, the island’s snake communities grew to be so problematic during a drought in the fourth century that the Roman Empress Helena , mother of Constantine the Great, called for shiploads of cats to be sent from Egypt to control the venomous reptiles.
The first feline imports were released in a particularly snake-infested area on the southeastern part of the Akrotiri Peninsula, an area that came to be known as Cape Gata (Cape Cat in Greek).
The cape today is still home to the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats , a place where legend says that monks encouraged newly arrived Egyptian cats to hunt snakes.
Today, Cyprus has as many cats as people, with more than one million of the feline predators stalking the island.
The handful of nuns who now live in the monastery still care for hundreds of cats, according to the St. Nicholas Center .

articles.title: Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars
paras: Science Observatory Team Multimedia News More 3 min read
This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image provides a lesson in galactic history.

The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer, Charles Messier , who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier’s time.
M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus.
M30 is a globular cluster : a roughly spherical grouping of stars containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars.
These clusters generally reside on the outskirts of galaxies, orbiting within a vast, diffuse region called the halo like a swarm of moths around a lightbulb.
Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters, the nearest of which is about 6,000 light-years away.
These clusters are impressively ancient: astronomers estimate their ages are between 11.5 to 13.5 billion years, making certain globular clusters nearly as old as the universe itself.
Globular clusters have long played an important role in helping us learn about our galaxy.
More than a century ago, astronomer Harlow Shapley used observations of a particular type of variable star to measure the locations of and distances to dozens of globular clusters within our galaxy.
His work showed that the Sun is not in the center of our galaxy, and that the galactic center lies toward the constellation Sagittarius.
(His distance measurements were incorrect, however, and he concluded that our galaxy is about twice as large as it really is.)
Today, astronomers continue to learn about our galaxy by observing globular clusters.
Because globular clusters are so ancient, they can give us clues about how our galaxy developed long ago.
Globular clusters that formed within our galaxy can act as time capsules, preserving the original chemistry of our young galaxy.
However, it’s possible that not all globular clusters that orbit within our galaxy today formed there.
Researchers have discovered that M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the direction opposite from the way our galaxy spins.
This may mean that these clusters did not form within our galaxy at all.
Instead, our Milky Way galaxy may have captured them in the distant past!
Hubble has observed M30 multiple times.

A previously released image of M30 featured data from Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and was part of an observing program (# 10775 ; PI: Sarajedini) that surveyed dozens of Milky Way globular clusters in red and near-infrared light, revealing stars down to just 20% of the mass of the Sun.

A more recent program (# 13297 ; PI: Piotto) returned to M30 and other globular clusters in our galaxy, this time observing the clusters with Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 and using three filters that captured bluer light.

This program collected data that was critical for studying exotic objects like “ blue straggler ” stars as well as for investigating the multiple populations of stars that can inhabit a single globular cluster.
More recently, Hubble’s ACS viewed many of these globular clusters again.

Those observations were part of a program (# 16298 , PI: Libralato) that looked at how different populations of stars in globular clusters moved over the 15 years since Hubble first observed them — a feat made possible by Hubble’s longevity and ability to discern fantastically small details in distant objects.
The image above was created with data from all three observing programs and includes the wide range of wavelengths Hubble can see — ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light.
Each wavelength helps us better understand how these groups of stars formed and evolved.
Claire Andreoli NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center , Greenbelt, MD claire.andreoli@nasa.gov
Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.
These jewels of the night sky offer us a glimpse at the lifecycle of stars.
Hubble’s most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.

articles.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
paras: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies.
The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight.
The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.

“The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“Its modular design and ability to rapidly swap internal and external payloads will keep our teams flying, learning, and moving quickly from one experiment to the next.
We expect her first flight under the NASA banner within the next two years, and X-70 is just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics.
This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly.”

The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles).
These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.

“For decades, NASA Aeronautics has used X-planes to develop technologies that advance aviation,” said Laurie Grindle, director of the Aeronautics Division within NASA’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate.
“It’s exciting to bring on another X-plane to accelerate and drive aeronautics research.”
The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America’s leadership in aviation.

From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today’s X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight.
With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.

articles.title: NASA Shares Plans to Accelerate Artemis, Return to Moon
paras: In an update on Oct. 23, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and other agency leaders shared the agency’s path to returning Americans to the lunar surface in 2028.

Agency leadership provided updates on the previously announced acceleration plans for the Artemis program, advancing toward the agency’s Artemis III test flight in 2027 and Artemis IV Moon landing mission in 2028.

Building on the priorities announced at Ignition earlier this year, NASA leadership shared the agency’s significant progress across its missions, working with industry partners to test critical capabilities, reduce risk, and build toward a sustained American presence on the Moon.
“This is a very energized NASA, and these updates are only a small part of that story.
We are bringing extreme focus to the mission to ensure delivery of world-changing outcomes as quickly, safely, affordably, and successfully as possible,” said Isaacman.

“NASA is driving outcomes to make Moon missions a reality, and we’re not waiting for others to bring their plans to us — the campaign must move with urgency as strategic competitors pursue a permanent presence beyond Earth.”

The agency shared details of the Artemis III mission, which will test rendezvous, docking, and operations between NASA’s Orion spacecraft and lunar lander test vehicles from SpaceX and Blue Origin in Earth orbit.
Four astronauts will fly aboard Orion, launched on NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket, for a planned 14-day mission in Earth orbit to reduce risk ahead of the Artemis IV moon landing mission.

The Artemis III mission will unfold in sequence: Blue Origin will launch a Blue Moon lander test article into Earth orbit, SLS will launch Orion and its crew, docking with the Blue Moon lander test article, then SpaceX will launch a Version 3 Starship lander test article while Orion will undock from Blue Moon and dock with Starship.
The Oct. 23 updates follow other recent updates about the Artemis missions.
Hardware for Artemis III is on track, with processing timelines sharply reduced by about half.
NASA also redesigned, built, and tested a critical fuel-line component in-house in five months, at roughly a tenth of the cost of an earlier outside-vendor estimate.

“NASA should be expected to do this kind of work, and we have some of the best technical knowledge in the world on rocket hardware and operations to do it,” said Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager.
“It’s an example of how we are rebuilding our core competencies and developing centers of excellence in technical functions instead of continuing to outsource expertise.”
For the agency’s Artemis IV mission in 2028, astronauts will launch aboard Orion on the SLS rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop lunar landers to carry those astronauts to the Moon’s surface.
Both companies have redesigned their approaches to simplify the missions and make them more efficient and flexible as compared to previous mission designs.
SpaceX’s Starship will refuel in Earth orbit, rendezvous with Orion, and then carry the spacecraft toward the Moon.
Blue Origin’s approach involves transfer stages in Earth orbit to push its Blue Moon Mark 2 lander toward the Moon, where it will meet Orion in a closer lunar orbit before descending to the surface.
Both SpaceX and Blue Origin are targeting to be able to support a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

For Artemis IV, NASA is pursuing two upper-stage options for the SLS rocket: its current stage, the interim cryogenic propulsion stage; and a stretched version of ULA’s Centaur V which can carry more propellant.
Pursuing both options ensures NASA is maintaining flexibility and preventing single-point dependency.
NASA also announced plans with spacesuit provider Axiom Space to develop a second, lighter suit design called the “Sortie suit” to enable the first moonwalks.
The Sortie suit will not replace Axiom’s primary suit, which will be used for longer, more demanding missions in the future.
The Sortie suit is roughly half the weight of the larger suit and lets NASA move faster on the earliest surface missions.
As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions at the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before.

In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

articles.title: TB 26-10 Printed Circuit Board Assembly Chip Resistor Body Cracking
paras: For more information, contact Joel W.
Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov .
Chip resistors are widely used in NASA projects, yet cases of alumina substrate cracking during environmental testing are rare.
Two instances of thick-film chip resistor cracking were observed during thermal cycling after vibration, with fractures occurring across the short axis due to bending.
Failure analyses ruled out defective lots and fatigue, identifying board flexure, component orientation, excessive solder, and mounting stresses as contributing factors.

The bulletin recommends careful component placement, finite element analysis, controlled solder fillet height, thorough inspection, and functional thermal shock testing to mitigate flexure-induced cracking risks in ceramic body components on printed circuit boards.

Background The NESC noted historical lack of reported cases of chip resistors’ alumina substrate cracking during vibration and thermal cycling, although chip resistors are ubiquitous across NASA projects.
Two instances of thick film chip resistor body cracking were observed during environmental acceptance testing on printed circuit board assemblies.
Both failures occurred during thermal cycling after vibration testing, exhibiting intermittent open circuit failures at hot dwell temperatures that recovered at room temperature.
Transverse fracture occurred at the mid-span of each resistor, running parallel to the terminations.
The two resistors were installed in similar locations near the edge of the boards on two identical boards.
Cracks in failed resistors were along the short axis of the resistor due to apparent bending of the resistors, Figure 1.
Resistors showed no signs of pre-existing defects.
Causal Relationships Initial theories pointed to vibration-induced damage of potentially defective resistors since both resistors came from the same production lot.

However, the resistor lot not only meets the requirements of procurement specification MIL-PRF-55342 but additional tests were performed and did not reveal any direct evidence of a defective resistor lot.
There was no evidence of an elevated risk of defective resistors within the production lot.
Failure Analyses Independent failure analyses concluded that the cracked chip resistors were due to bending/tensile failures.
There was no clear-cut root cause or visible defect identifying a crack initiation site.
Both resistors exhibited a single, straight crack across the short axis (perpendicular to the long axis), indicating a bending/tensile failure without twisting.
The damage signatures are not consistent with cyclic fatigue, likely ruling out fatigue failure during vibration.

In addition, NESC independent optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Figure 2, of both resistors did not identify any clear flaw locations for fatigue damage initiation and progression; therefore, the possibility of defective resistors as well as fatigue vibration as the root cause becomes unlikely.

Cause Conclusions No direct root cause was identified, but contributing factors leading to increased design consideration needed for large footprint ceramic components located near the edges of a printed circuit board that can lead to stress cracks due to manufacturing or installation bow/twist of the printed circuit board include:

articles.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
paras: Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands.
Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October.

When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands.
At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea.
In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year.
The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain.

In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms .

These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.”
Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis .

Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions.

In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track.

Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses.
Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas .
“One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
“It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said.
In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added.
“But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said.

Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season.
Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan.

When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025 , but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports .

Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman , following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October.
The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added.
Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970 , according to Thoman.
Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions.
The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added.
El Niño is a climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific.

In the Northwest Pacific, the phenomenon tends to cause storms to more readily curve northward rather than continuing westward to East Asia and Southeast Asia, some experts say , bringing more storms toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula.

articles.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
paras: Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon!
November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky!
The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th.
Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate.
Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile.
Next up are the Leonids.
For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets.
Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer.
To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can.
Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early.
On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together.
They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side.
Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby.
Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye.
They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side.
Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways.
This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it!
If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer.
And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation.
Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager .
On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon.
Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes.
When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average – though the difference can be subtle.
This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January.
Look east around sunset to watch it rise.
It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon.

articles.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
paras: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight.
Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis.
Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery.
Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space.
As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts.
Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit.

For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth.
On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F.
Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade.

NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia.

The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas.
The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962.
In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B.
Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation.
The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston.
The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963.
Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs.
Project Management Building Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964.
Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2.
The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974.
Neutral buoyancy spacewalk training The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966.
In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training..
To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980.

Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities.
Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Building 37) To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37.
Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967.

The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned.
Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017.
Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory.
Spacecraft mockup training facilities (Building 9) Construction of Building 9 began in December 1965 and finished in March 1967.
The building initially housed the Technical Services Facility.
In April 1969, workers converted a portion of the building to include a mock lunar surface scene, complete with a mockup of a Lunar Module, used by Apollo 11 astronauts.
To support the space shuttle program, workers completed an addition that housed the Mockup and Integration Laboratory in September 1974.
Astronauts for all 135 shuttle missions used the mockups for training.
An extension on the northwest side of thebuilding begun in 1986 and completed in 1988.
It received mockups of Space Station Freedom and later of the International Space Station, and the building was renamed the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility.
Today, the facility also houses training mockups of NASA’s Orion spacecraft, commercial mockups, and the Active Response Gravity Offload System, known as ARGOS.

Mission Simulation and Training Facility (Building 5) Construction of Building 5 , the Mission Simulation and Training Facility completed inApril 1965 and began supporting missions beginning with Gemini IV in June 1965.
The building originally contained the Gemini spacecraft simulator and a Gemini translation and docking simulator.
Apollo program simulators, including a command module and lunar module simulator, began arriving in December 1965.
From 1967 and 1978, astronauts used the Water Immersion Facility for spacewalk training.
In the early 1970s, the building also housed full-scale, high-fidelity trainers and simulators of Skylab’s components, which all nine Skylab astronauts used for mission training.
In the late 1970s, the facility underwent major renovations to support the space shuttle program, with the addition of fixed base and motion base simulators.

The Space Station Training Facility addition, completed in 1991, supported first Space Station Freedom and now International Space Station crew training, and also contains Orion and Starliner simulators.

Mission Control Center Construction of Building 30 housing the Mission Control Center began in June 1963 and finished in November 1964, with technicians installing the real-time computer in April 1964 and the first employees moving in two months later.
The center initially housed two mission operations control rooms to support Gemini and Apollo missions and simulations.
By January 1965, the center monitored the uncrewed Gemini 2 mission and the crewed Gemini 3 mission in a flight following mode.
In June 1965, Houston had full control of Gemini IV and has controlled each of NASA’s human space flight missions ever since.
The control center received a major upgrade to its computer systems in the mid-1970s to support upcoming space shuttle flights.
On April 4, 2011, the building was renamed the Christopher C.
Kraft, Jr. Mission Control Center, in honor of the man who created the concepts still in use today in human spaceflight control.
The control center continues to support the space station around the clock as well as Artemis missions taking humans back to the Moon.

articles.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
paras: For more information, contact Joel W.
Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov .
An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform.
When the complete force and response are measured accurately, crest ripples and separated contacts remain known inputs.
Force shape changes excitation, but does not inherently invalidate the record.
Adequacy depends on measurement accuracy, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, and coverage of the test objective.
Background: What the Hammer Actually Measures Hammer tests support modal analysis [2–4] and can precede pyroshock testing [6].
Figure 1 compares a half-sine, maintained-contact rippling, and separated contacts.
During a zero-force interval, the structure continues to vibrate; re-contact acts on that vibration.
If an exact model and test article receive the same force and initial conditions, uniqueness gives identical responses for each bounded measured history.
An approximate model can show different errors as inputs excite different frequencies, amplitudes, or nonlinear states.
See [1] for the exact-model derivation.
Analysis: A Half-Sine Is Broadband, but Not Flat Figure 2 shows that a finite half-sine is broadband but contains spectral zeros at f/fo = 3, 5, 7, …, with fo = 1/(2T) for pulse duration T.
Its appearance alone cannot establish adequate excitation.
Analysis: Spectral Content Is Determined by the Measured Force History Figure 3 normalizes each spectrum to its own DC value.
Crest rippling adds content and can fill half-sine notches.
Timing between separated contacts creates deterministic interference.
For adequacy, inspect the unnormalized measured spectrum and response signal-to-noise ratio.

Recommended Practice: Evaluate Test Adequacy Against the Intended Objective • Measure the complete applied force with adequate bandwidth, calibration, dynamic range, and time synchronization. • Verify that the response measurements have adequate bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio and are not clipped or saturated. • Confirm that the excitation covers the frequency, amplitude, and nonlinear-response ranges required by the intended test objective. • Reject or repeat a test only for an identified measurement, excitation, or coverage deficiency.
Conclusion Half-sine appearance neither establishes validity nor guarantees adequacy.
Judge each hammer test by its purpose and by accurate, complete force and response measurements over the required range.
